source_text: –Ἀλλὰ πένητα λέγεις σαυτόν· κἀγὼ συντίθεμαι. Πένης γάρ ἐστιν ὁ πολλῶν ἐνδεής. Πολλῶν δὲ ὑμᾶς ἐνδεεῖς ποιεῖ τὸ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀκόρεστον. Τοῖς δέκα ταλάντοις δέκα ἕτερα προστιθέναι σπουδάζεις· ἐπειδὰν εἴκοσι γένηται, ἄλλα τοσαῦτα ἐπιζητεῖς, καὶ ἀεί σοι τὸ προστιθέμενον, οὐχὶ τὴν ὁρμὴν ἵστησιν, ἀλλ' ἀναφλέγει τὴν ὄρεξιν. Ὥσπερ γὰρ τοῖς μεθύουσιν ἀφορμὴ τοῦ πίνειν ἡ προσθήκη τοῦ οἴνου γίνεται, οὕτω καὶ οἱ νεόπλουτοι, πολλὰ κτησάμενοι, πλειόνων ἐπιθυμοῦσι, τῷ ἀεὶ προστιθεμένῳ τὴν νόσον τρέφοντες, καὶ περιτρέπεται αὐτοῖς ἡ σπουδὴ πρὸς τὸ ἐναντίον. Οὐ γὰρ εὐφραίνει αὐτοὺς τὰ παρόντα τοσαῦτα ὄντα, ὅσον λυπεῖ τὰ ἐνδέοντα ἅπερ ἂν αὐτοῖς ἐλλείπειν ὑπόθωνται· ὥστε ἀεὶ τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῖς ταῖς μερίμναις ἐκτήκεσθαι, πρὸς τὸ ὑπερβάλλον τὴν ἅμιλλαν ποιουμένοις. Δέον γὰρ εὐφραίνεσθαι καὶ χάριν ἔχειν, τοσούτων ὄντας εὐπορωτέρους· οἱ δὲ δυσφο ροῦσιν καὶ ὀδυνῶνται, ὅτι ἑνός που ἢ δευτέρου τῶν ὑπερπλουτούντων ἀπολιμπάνονται. Ὅταν τοῦτον τὸν πλούσιον καταλάβωσιν, εὐθὺς τῷ πλου σιωτέρῳ παρισωθῆναι φιλονεικοῦσιν· κἂν ἐπ' ἐκεῖνον φθάσωσιν, ἐπὶ τὸν ἄλλον τὴν σπουδὴν μεταφέρουσιν. Ὥσπερ γὰρ οἱ τὰς κλίμακας ἀναβαίνοντες, ἀεὶ πρὸς τὴν ὑπερκειμένην βαθμίδα τὸ ἴχνος αἴροντες, οὐ πρό τερον ἵστανται πρὶν ἂν τῆς ἄκρας ἐφίκωνται· οὕτω καὶ οὗτοι οὐ παύονται τῆς κατὰ τὴν δυναστείαν ὁρμῆς, ἕως ἂν ὑψωθέντες, ἀπὸ μετεώρου τοῦ πτώματος ἑαυτοὺς καταῤῥάξωσιν. Τὴν σελευκίδα τὸ ὄρνεον ἐπ' εὐεργεσίᾳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀκόρεστον εἶναι ὁ κτίστης τῶν ὅλων ἐμηχανήσατο· σὺ δὲ ἐπὶ βλάβῃ τῶν πολλῶν ἀκόρεστον εἶναι ὁ κτίστης τῶν ὅλων ἐμηχανήσατο· σὺ δὲ ἐπὶ βλάβῃ τῶν πολλῶν ἀκόρεστον τὴν σεαυτοῦ ψυχὴν κατεσκεύασας. Ὅσα βλέπει ὀφθαλμὸς, τοσούτων ἐπιθυμεῖ ὁ πλεονέκτης· Οὐ πλησθήσεται ὀφθαλμὸς τοῦ ὁρᾷν· καὶ οὐ κορεσθήσεται φιλάργυρος τοῦ λαμβάνειν. Ὁ ᾅδης οὐκ εἶπεν· Ἀρκεῖ, οὐδὲ ὁ πλεονέκτης εἶπέ ποτε· Ἀρκεῖ. Πότε χρήσῃ τοῖς παροῦσι; πότε ἀπολαύσεις αὐτῶν, ἀεὶ τοῖς πόνοις τῆς κτήσεως συνεχόμενος; Οὐαὶ οἱ συνάπτοντες οἰκίαν πρὸς οἰκίαν, καὶ ἀγρὸν πρὸς ἀγρὸν ἐγγίζοντες, ἵνα τοῦ πλησίον ἀφέλωνταί τι· Σὺ δὲ τί ποιεῖς; Οὐ προφασίζῃ μυρία, ἵνα λάβῃς τὰ τοῦ πλησίον; Ἐπισκοτεῖ μοι, φησὶν, ἡ τοῦ γείτονος οἰκία, θορύβους ἐνίησιν, ἢ τὸ πλανώμενον ὑποδέχεται, ἢ ὅ τι ἂν τύχῃ αἰτιασάμενος, περιελαύνων, καὶ ἐξωθῶν, καὶ ἕλκων ἀεὶ, καὶ σπαράσσων, οὐ πρότερον παύεται, πρὶν ἂν ἐπαγάγῃ αὐτοῖς ἀνάγκην μετα ναστάσεως. Τί τὸν Ναβουθὲ τὸν Ἰεζραηλίτην ἀπέκτεινεν; Οὐχ ἡ τοῦ Ἀχαὰβ ἐπιθυμία τοῦ ἀμπελῶνος; Πονηρὸς ἐν πόλει σύνοικος, πονηρὸς ἐν ἀγροῖς, ὁ πλεονέκτης. Ἡ θάλασσα οἶδεν τὰ ὅρια αὐτῆς· ἡ νὺξ οὐχ ὑπερβαίνει ὁροθεσίας ἀρχαίας. Ὁ δὲ πλεονέκτης οὐκ αἰδεῖται χρόνον, οὐ γνωρίζει ὅρον, οὐ συγχωρεῖ ἀκολουθίαν διαδοχῆς, ἀλλὰ μιμεῖται τοῦ πυρὸς τὴν βίαν· πάντα ἐπιλαμβάνει, πάντα ἐπινέμεται. Καὶ ὥσπερ οἱ ποταμοὶ, ἐκ μικρᾶς τῆς πρώτης ἀρχῆς ὁρμηθέντες, εἶτα ταῖς κατ' ὀλίγον προσθήκαις ἀνυπόστατον λαβόντες τὴν αὔξησιν, τῷ βιαίῳ τῆς φορᾶς τὸ ἐνιστάμενον παρασύρουσιν· οὕτω καὶ οἱ ἐπὶ μέγα τῆς δυνάμεως προελθόντες, ἐκ τῶν ἤδη καταδυναστευθέντων τὴν τοῦ πλείονας ἀδικεῖν δύναμιν προσλαμβάνοντες, τοῖς προηδικημένοις τοὺς λειπομένους καταδουλοῦνται, καὶ γίνεται αὐτοῖς δυνάμεως αὔξησις ἡ περιουσία τῆς πονηρίας. Οἱ γὰρ προπεπονθότες κακῶς, ἠναγκασμένην αὐτοῖς παρεχόμενοι τὴν βοή θειαν, τὰς καθ' ἑτέρων βλάβας καὶ ἀδικίας συνεκπονοῦσιν. Ποῖος γὰρ γείτων, ποῖος σύνοικος, τίς συναλλάκτης οὐ παρασύρεται; Οὐδὲν ὑφίσταται τὴν βίαν τοῦ πλούτου· Πάντα ὑποκύπτει τῇ τυραννίδι, πάντα ὑποπτήσσει τὴν δυναστείαν, πλείονα λόγον ἑκάστου τῶν ἠδικημένων ἔχοντος μὴ προσπαθεῖν τι κακὸν, ἢ δίκην λαβεῖν ὑπὲρ τῶν φθασάντων. Ἐπάγει τὰ ζεύγη τῶν βοῶν, ἀροτριᾷ, κατασπείρει, θερίζει τὰ μὴ προσήκοντα. Ἐὰν ἀντείπῃς, αἱ πληγαί· ἐὰν ὀδύρῃ, ὕβρεων γραφαὶ, ἀγώγιμος εἶ, οἰκήσεις τὸ δεσμωτήριον, οἱ συκοφάνται εὐτρεπεῖς, εἰς τὸν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ζῇν κίνδυνον καθιστῶντες. Ἀγαπήσεις, καὶ ἄλλο τι προσδοὺς, ἀπηλλάχθαι πραγμάτων.
thought_title: Insatiable desire makes the rich poor
orientation: Basil is answering the rich person's excuse that he is poor, showing that insatiable desire, not lack, makes him poor, and then describing how the greedy oppress their neighbors.
pass_a_gloss: But you say that you yourself are poor; and I agree. For a poor man is one who lacks many things. And the insatiable nature of desire makes you lack many things. You are eager to add ten other talents to the ten talents; when they become twenty, you seek another equal amount, and always the thing added to you does not stop the impulse, but kindles the appetite. For just as for those who are drunk the addition of wine becomes an occasion for drinking, so also the newly rich, having acquired much, desire more, feeding the disease with what is always added, and their eagerness turns around to the opposite. For the things present, being so many, do not gladden them as much as the things lacking grieve them, whatever they suppose is missing for them; so that their soul is always wasted away by anxieties, as they make their rivalry for what exceeds. For though they ought to rejoice and be grateful, being more well-provided than so many, they are distressed and pained, because they fall short of one or a second of the very rich. Whenever they overtake this rich man, immediately they strive to be made equal to the richer one; and if they reach that one, they transfer their eagerness to another. For just as those climbing ladders, always lifting their foot to the step above, do not stop before they reach the top; so also these do not cease from the impulse according to power, until, having been raised high, they hurl themselves down from a lofty fall. The Creator of all things devised the seleucis bird to be insatiable for the benefit of humans; but you have made your own soul insatiable for the harm of many. As many things as the eye sees, so many the greedy person desires; The eye will not be satisfied with seeing; and the money-lover will not be satisfied with taking. Hades did not say: Enough, nor did the greedy person ever say: Enough. When will you use the things present? When will you enjoy them, always held fast by the labors of acquisition? Woe to those who join house to house, and bring field near to field, in order that they may take something from the neighbor; But what do you do? Do you not make ten thousand pretexts, in order that you may take the things of the neighbor? The neighbor's house, he says, casts a shadow on me, it sends in disturbances, or it receives the wanderer, or whatever accusation he happens to make, driving around, and pushing out, and always dragging, and tearing, he does not stop before he brings upon them the necessity of removal. What killed Naboth the Jezreelite? Was it not Ahab's desire for the vineyard? An evil fellow-dweller in the city, an evil one in the fields, is the greedy person. The sea knows its boundaries; the night does not overstep ancient limits. But the greedy person does not respect time, does not recognize a boundary, does not allow the succession of inheritance, but imitates the force of fire; it seizes all things, it devours all things. And just as rivers, having rushed from a small first beginning, then having taken an irresistible increase by the additions little by little, sweep away what stands in the way by the violence of their course; so also those who have advanced to great power, taking from those already oppressed the power to wrong more people, enslave those who remain to those already wronged, and the abundance of wickedness becomes for them an increase of power. For those who have previously suffered evil, providing forced help to them, jointly accomplish the harms and injustices against others. For what neighbor, what fellow-dweller, what business partner is not swept away? Nothing withstands the force of wealth; All things bow to the tyranny, all things cower before the power, since each of the wronged has more reason not to suffer some evil than to get justice for what has already happened. He brings in the yokes of oxen, he plows, he sows, he harvests what does not belong to him. If you speak against him, blows; if you lament, indictments for insults, you are liable to arrest, you will dwell in the prison, the sycophants are ready, placing you in danger for your life. You will prefer, giving something more, to be rid of troubles.

choices.term: Πένης γάρ ἐστιν ὁ πολλῶν ἐνδεής
choices.english: For a poor man is one who lacks many things
choices.why: Keeps the definitional force of γάρ and the present tense of ἐστιν; 'lacks many things' preserves the genitive πολλῶν with ἐνδεής.
rejected: For the poor man is he who is in need of many things

choices.why: Renders the articular adjective ἀκόρεστον as a substantive with 'nature' to make the abstract quality clear in English.
Captures the compound νεόπλουτος (newly + rich) as a single English phrase.
Keeps the Greek name σελευκίς transliterated, since the exact species is uncertain; 'bird' clarifies the apposition.

choices.english: The eye will not be satisfied with seeing
choices.why: Literal future passive of πλησθήσεται with the articular infinitive τοῦ ὁρᾶν rendered as 'with seeing.'
rejected: The eye is not satisfied with seeing
The eye will not be filled with seeing

choices.term: Ἀγαπήσεις, καὶ ἄλλο τι προσδοὺς, ἀπηλλάχθαι πραγμάτων
choices.english: You will prefer, giving something more, to be rid of troubles
choices.why: Ἀγαπήσεις is future of ἀγαπάω meaning 'you will prefer/love to'; the aorist participle προσδούς is rendered as 'giving something more'; the perfect infinitive ἀπηλλάχθαι as 'to be rid of.'
rejected: You will choose, giving something more, to be rid of the trouble
You will love, giving something extra, to be freed from affairs

pass_b_english: But you say you are poor, and I agree. For a poor man is one who lacks many things, and the insatiable nature of desire makes you lack many things. You are eager to add ten more talents to your ten; when they become twenty, you seek another twenty, and what is added never stops your impulse but kindles your appetite. Just as for drunkards the addition of wine becomes an occasion for more drinking, so the newly rich, after acquiring much, desire more, feeding the disease with each addition, and their eagerness turns to the opposite. For what they have, great as it is, does not gladden them as much as what they lack grieves them, whatever they imagine is missing; so their soul is always wasting away with cares, as they carry their rivalry beyond all measure. They ought to rejoice and give thanks for being wealthier than so many, but they are distressed and tormented because they fall short of one or two of the super-rich. When they overtake this rich man, they immediately contend to equal the richer one; and if they reach him, they transfer their eagerness to the next. Just as those climbing ladders always lift their foot to the step above and do not stop until they reach the top, so these people do not cease their rush for power until, raised high, they hurl themselves down from a great height. The Creator of all things devised the seleucis bird to be insatiable for the benefit of human beings; but you have devised your own soul to be insatiable for the harm of many. Whatever the eye sees, the greedy person desires. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the money-lover with taking (Ecclesiastes 5:10 [4:8 LXX]). Hades never said, “Enough,” and the greedy person never said, “Enough.” When will you use what you have? When will you enjoy it, always gripped by the labors of acquisition? Woe to those who join house to house and bring field near field, so that they may take something from their neighbor (Isaiah 5:8). And what do you do? Do you not make countless pretexts to take your neighbor’s property? “My neighbor’s house blocks my light,” he says, “it causes disturbances,” or “it shelters runaways,” or whatever charge he happens to make, driving out, pushing out, always dragging and tearing, he does not stop until he brings upon them the necessity of moving away. What killed Naboth the Jezreelite? Was it not Ahab’s desire for the vineyard? A wicked fellow citizen in the city, wicked in the fields, is the greedy person. The sea knows its boundaries; the night does not overstep its ancient limits. But the greedy person does not respect time, does not recognize a boundary, does not allow the order of succession, but imitates the force of fire: it seizes everything, it devours everything. And just as rivers, rushing from a small first beginning, then with gradual additions taking on irresistible growth, sweep away whatever stands in their path by the violence of their current, so those who have advanced to great power, taking from those already oppressed the ability to wrong more people, enslave the remaining ones through those already wronged, and their abundance of wickedness becomes for them an increase of power. For those who have already suffered evil, providing forced assistance, join in carrying out the harms and injustices against others. For what neighbor, what fellow citizen, what business partner is not swept away? Nothing withstands the violence of wealth. Everything bows to its tyranny, everything cowers before its power, since each of the wronged has more reason not to suffer again than to get justice for what has already happened. He drives his teams of oxen, plows, sows, and harvests what does not belong to him. If you speak against it, there are beatings; if you lament, charges of insult; you are hauled away, you will live in prison, the sycophants are ready, as they put you in danger of your life. You will be glad, by giving something more, to be rid of troubles.
notes: The source has a duplicated clause: 'σὺ δὲ ἐπὶ βλάβῃ τῶν πολλῶν ἀκόρεστον εἶναι ὁ κτίστης τῶν ὅλων ἐμηχανήσατο· σὺ δὲ ἐπὶ βλάβῃ τῶν πολλῶν ἀκόρεστον τὴν σεαυτοῦ ψυχὴν κατεσκεύασας.' The first clause appears to be a dittography or scribal error, since it repeats the Creator's action before the contrast with 'you.' The gloss renders the second clause as the intended contrast.

problems.quote: enslave the rest to those already wronged
problems.why: Greek means they enslave the remaining ones 'by means of' or 'using' those already wronged, not 'to' them.
problems.fix: enslave the remaining ones through those already wronged

problems.quote: since each of the wronged has more reason not to suffer further evil than to get justice for what has already happened
problems.source_quote: πλείονα λόγον ἑκάστου τῶν ἠδικημένων ἔχοντος μὴ προσπαθεῖν τι κακὸν, ἢ δίκην λαβεῖν ὑπὲρ τῶν φθασάντων
problems.why: Greek says each wronged person has more reason to avoid suffering evil than to obtain justice; English inverts the comparison logic.
problems.fix: each of the wronged having more reason not to suffer some evil than to get justice for past wrongs

problems.quote: The Creator of all things devised the seleucis bird to be insatiable for the benefit of human beings; but you have made your own soul insatiable for the harm of many.
problems.source_quote: σὺ δὲ ἐπὶ βλάβῃ τῶν πολλῶν ἀκόρεστον τὴν σεαυτοῦ ψυχὴν κατεσκεύασας
problems.why: The source repeats 'ὁ κτίστης τῶν ὅλων ἐμηχανήσατο' twice, creating a parallel: God made the bird insatiable for benefit; YOU made your soul insatiable for harm. The English drops the second divine agency clause, flattening the contrast.
problems.fix: The Creator of all devised the seleucis bird to be insatiable for humanity's benefit; but you, devising your soul insatiable for the harm of many…
problems.ruling: Source repeats 'ὁ κτίστης τῶν ὅλων ἐμηχανήσατο' twice; English drops second clause, breaking parallel.

problems.quote: The eye will not be satisfied with seeing (Ecclesiastes 4:8)
problems.why: The quote matches Ecclesiastes 1:8, not 4:8. LXX Ecclesiastes 1:8 has this exact wording.
problems.fix: The eye will not be satisfied with seeing (Ecclesiastes 1:8)
problems.ruling: Source quote 'Οὐ πλησθήσεται ὀφθαλμός τοῦ ὁρᾷν' matches LXX Ecclesiastes 1:8, not 4:8.

problems.quote: You would prefer, giving something more, to be rid of troubles
problems.source_quote: Ἀγαπήσεις, καὶ ἄλλο τι προσδοὺς, ἀπηλλάχθαι πραγμάτων
problems.why: Ἀγαπήσεις is future indicative ('you will love/like it'), not conditional 'would prefer'; it's a grim prediction, not a choice offered.
problems.fix: You will be glad, giving something more, to be rid of troubles
problems.ruling: Ἀγαπήσεις is future indicative 'you will love it,' not conditional 'would prefer'; changes meaning.

fixed: Corrected 'enslave the rest to those already wronged' to 'enslave the remaining ones through those already wronged' to reflect the instrumental dative τοῖς προηδικημένοις.

Corrected 'since each of the wronged has more reason not to suffer further evil than to get justice for what has already happened' to 'since each of the wronged has more reason not to suffer some evil than to get justice for what has already happened' to match the Greek μὴ προσπαθεῖν τι κακὸν and avoid the inverted comparison.

Restored the parallel divine agency clause in the seleucis bird sentence by changing 'but you have made your own soul insatiable' to 'but you have devised your own soul to be insatiable', reflecting the source's repetition of the verb μηχανάομαι.
Corrected the scripture reference from Ecclesiastes 4:8 to Ecclesiastes 1:8, which matches the LXX wording Οὐ πλησθήσεται ὀφθαλμὸς τοῦ ὁρᾷν.
Changed 'You would prefer' to 'You will be glad' to render the future indicative Ἀγαπήσεις as a grim prediction rather than a conditional preference.

problems.quote: You will be glad, giving something more, to be rid of troubles
problems.source_quote: Ἀγαπήσεις, καὶ ἄλλο τι προσδοὺς, ἀπηλλάχθαι πραγμάτων
problems.why: Ἀγαπήσεις is future indicative of ἀγαπάω (you will love), not 'be glad'; the sense is ironic: 'you will love, by giving something more, to be rid of troubles'—i.e., bribery.
problems.fix: You will love, by giving something more, to be rid of troubles.

problems.quote: since each of the wronged has more reason not to suffer some evil than to get justice for what has already happened
problems.source_quote: πλείονα λόγον ἑκάστου τῶν ἠδικημένων ἔχοντος μὴ προσπαθεῖν τι κακὸν, ἢ δίκην λαβεῖν ὑπὲρ τῶν φθασάντων
problems.why: μὴ προσπαθεῖν means 'not to suffer in addition/again,' not 'not to suffer some evil'; the wronged prefer avoiding further suffering over getting justice for past wrongs.
problems.fix: since each of the wronged has more reason not to suffer again than to get justice for what has already happened.

problems.quote: he does not stop until he forces them to move away
problems.source_quote: οὐ πρότερον παύεται, πρὶν ἂν ἐπαγάγῃ αὐτοῖς ἀνάγκην μεταναστάσεως
problems.why: The English loses the key noun ἀνάγκην (necessity/compulsion): 'he does not stop until he brings upon them the necessity of moving away.'
problems.fix: he does not stop until he brings upon them the necessity of moving away.

problems.quote: and their eagerness turns against them
problems.source_quote: περιτρέπεται αὐτοῖς ἡ σπουδὴ πρὸς τὸ ἐναντίον
problems.why: Source says eagerness turns 'toward the opposite,' i.e., reverses into harm, not merely 'against them.'
problems.fix: and their eagerness turns to the opposite
problems.ruling: πρὸς τὸ ἐναντίον means 'toward the opposite,' not merely 'against them'—meaning changed.

problems.quote: as they strive to surpass what lies beyond
problems.source_quote: πρὸς τὸ ὑπερβάλλον τὴν ἅμιλλαν ποιουμένοις
problems.why: Source means 'engaging in rivalry beyond measure,' not 'surpass what lies beyond.' Misreads the grammar.
problems.fix: as they carry their rivalry beyond all measure
problems.ruling: πρὸς τὸ ὑπερβάλλον τὴν ἅμιλλαν ποιουμένοις = 'engaging in rivalry with what surpasses,' misread as 'surpass what lies beyond.'

problems.quote: The eye will not be satisfied with seeing (Ecclesiastes 1:8)
problems.source_quote: Οὐ πλησθήσεται ὀφθαλμὸς τοῦ ὁρᾶν· καὶ οὐ κορεσθήσεται φιλάργυρος τοῦ λαμβάνειν
problems.why: The citation is Ecclesiastes 1:8, but the Greek quotes Ecclesiastes 5:10 (LXX 4:8): 'ὀφθαλμὸς οὐκ ἐμπλησθήσεται ὁρᾶν' and 'οὐδὲ πλησθήσεται φιλάργυρος τοῦ κτήσασθαι.'
problems.fix: The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the money-lover with taking (Ecclesiastes 5:10 [4:8 LXX]).
problems.ruling: Source quotes Ecclesiastes 5:10 (LXX 4:8), not 1:8; wrong scripture reference misleads the reader.

fixed: Ἀγαπήσεις is future of ἀγαπάω, 'you will love,' not 'be glad'; corrected to 'You will love, by giving something more, to be rid of troubles.'
μὴ προσπαθεῖν means 'not to suffer in addition/again,' not 'not to suffer some evil'; corrected to 'not to suffer again.'
The English omitted ἀνάγκην (necessity/compulsion); restored as 'the necessity of moving away.'
πρὸς τὸ ἐναντίον means 'toward the opposite,' not 'against them'; corrected to 'turns to the opposite.'
πρὸς τὸ ὑπερβάλλον τὴν ἅμιλλαν ποιουμένοις means 'engaging in rivalry beyond measure,' not 'strive to surpass what lies beyond'; corrected to 'carry their rivalry beyond all measure.'
The quotation is Ecclesiastes 5:10 (LXX 4:8), not 1:8; corrected citation and wording.

problems.quote: You will love, by giving something more, to be rid of troubles
problems.source_quote: Ἀγαπήσεις, καὶ ἄλλο τι προσδοὺς, ἀπηλλάχθαι πραγμάτων
problems.why: Misreads syntax: 'you will love to be rid of troubles, even by giving something more'—the oppressed must bribe to escape.
problems.fix: You would gladly give something more to be rid of troubles

problems.quote: the sycophants are ready, putting you in danger for your life.
problems.source_quote: οἱ συκοφάνται εὐτρεπεῖς, εἰς τὸν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ζῇν κίνδυνον καθιστῶντες.
problems.why: The subject of καθιστῶντες is the powerful oppressor, not the sycophants; the oppressor uses ready sycophants to put you in mortal danger.
problems.fix: the sycophants are ready, as he puts you in danger of your life.
problems.ruling: καθιστῶντες dative plural participle agrees with οἱ συκοφάνται, but context shows the oppressor (subject of surrounding verbs) uses them; 'putting' misattributes agency.

edits.old: You will love, by giving something more, to be rid of troubles.
edits.new: You will be glad, by giving something more, to be rid of troubles.

edits.old: the sycophants are ready, putting you in danger for your life.
edits.new: the sycophants are ready, as he puts you in danger of your life.

fixed: The first problem is real: the source 'Ἀγαπήσεις, καὶ ἄλλο τι προσδούς, ἀπηλλάχθαι πραγμάτων' means 'you will love to be rid of troubles, even by giving something more.' The English 'You will love, by giving something more, to be rid of troubles' is awkward and misplaces the emphasis. I changed 'love' to 'be glad' to better capture the sense of preferring to give something extra to escape trouble, while keeping the sentence natural.

The second problem is real: the source 'οἱ συκοφάνται εὐτρεπεῖς, εἰς τὸν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ζῆν κίνδυνον καθιστῶντες' has the participle 'καθιστῶντες' referring to the oppressor, not the sycophants. The oppressor uses ready sycophants to put you in mortal danger. I changed 'putting you in danger for your life' to 'as he puts you in danger of your life' to clarify the subject.

fixed.quote: as he puts you in danger of your life
fixed.fix: as they put you in danger of your life
fixed.note: The participle καθιστῶντες is plural and goes with οἱ συκοφάνται, so the informers, not 'he', put the victim's life in danger.

dismissed.why: Greek has φιλάργυρος (money-lover/avaricious person), but the glossary bans 'love of money' and specifies 'love of wealth' for φιλοπλουτία. However, φιλάργυρος is a different word. The English 'money-lover' is accurate for φιλάργυρος. Not reporting.
